Passive of Modals May and Might

We use the passive form to highlight the element that receives the action in a sentence instead of its subject (the doer of the action). Now, don't forget that modal verbs can also have their own passive form.

You use modals in the passive voice to change the intention of the sentence. Remember that both ‘may' as well as ‘might' express possibility in the future. In fact, ‘may' tends to imply the idea that something is more likely to occur than ‘might'. Furthermore, ‘might' tends to be perceived as the most formal one.

The structure that we follow to make sentences using the passive voice of the modal verbs ‘may' and ‘might' is:
Object of the sentence + may / might + be + action verb (in past participle) + (by + subject*) + complement.
*Remember that in the passive voice, you can omit the subject of the sentence; however, when you want to include it, you just have to mention it in this part of the sentence.

For example:
A data model might be used to organize all this information.
A meeting may be called to discuss data models.
The DBMS model might be developed by the designers.

Relational Tables
The relational database model is mainly made using a table to present all the information.

The relational table is successful because as it is organized logically, it is easier to understand; in fact, this model is logic-driven, which makes it more intuitive and natural. This type of model is composed by relations, or tables, that present rows (attributes) and columns. This distribution allows the data contained in them to be related with one another.
In the table, the rows represent a single entity (for example, a person), while the columns represent an attribute of that single entity. Then, each crossing represents a particular data value.

Mr. Goodman: Good morning! Before presenting the exam, we can make a short review of the topics we checked this week. Data models, for example, might be included in the exam.
Brian: Can we discuss what they are and do, please?
Mr. Goodman: Sure. Data models are really important for DBMS. These models basically shape the logical structures of the systems as well as provide abstraction qualities to the databases they work on.
Brian: I think a simpler explanation may be required…
Mr. Goodman: Okay. This model might be perceived as the pillar of the database as it shapes the way the information is linked within databases. Furthermore, it also plays a big role in how the system processes and stores data.

Brian: That's pretty clear now. Do you agree that by not covering ER models, this topic is incomplete?
Mr. Goodman: That is true. Now, making connections among world entities and attributes might be seen as one of the main advantages of using the entity relationship model. In fact, by not leaving aside two important concepts, we can get to understand this topic. Those concepts are entities, units with their own attributes called domains, and relationships, which are expressed through graphs showing mapping cardinalities.

Brian: Great! What about the relational data model?
Mr. Goodman: Well, that topic might be also included in the exam.
Brian: I remember that this model may be identified as one of the simplest and clearest models to use as it uses relational tables.
Mr. Goodman: That is correct. This model allows us to create and analyze inter-related tables; in other words, we can unequivocally check entities as well as their attributes. In fact, this model is the most scientific and clear out there.
